reconcile.note: John Gill argues Jesus rebukes only the Pharisees' private-revenge gloss on the lex talionis, not the Mosaic statute itself, which governed the civil magistrate alone.

discrepancy.note: Ingersoll charges that Christians who invoke the turn-the-other-cheek teaching still fall back on retaliatory warfare and even persecution.

quotes.text: for one who follows the Master who said that when smitten on one cheek you must turn the other, and who again and again enforced the idea that you must overcome evil with good, it is hardly consistent to declare that a civilized nation must of necessity adopt the warfare of savages.
quotes.attr: Robert G. Ingersoll (d. 1899), The Christian Religion, pt. III (1881), on Matthew 5:39.

quotes.text: Priests believing in the doctrine of universal forgiveness—priests who when smitten upon one cheek turned the other—carried with a kind of ferocious joy fagots to the feet of this incomparable man.
quotes.attr: Robert G. Ingersoll (d. 1899), The Christian Religion, pt. III (1881), on Matthew 5:39.

sides.snippet: eye for eye, tooth for tooth
sides.verseText: fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth; as he has injured someone, so shall it be done to him.

sides.snippet: don't resist him who is evil
sides.verseText: But I tell you, don't resist him who is evil; but whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also.
